title: Introduction to Indian Accounting Standards
outcomes: Explain why India moved from AS to Ind AS and how Ind AS relate to IFRS.
Describe how Ind AS are developed, notified, numbered and structured.
Apply the Ind AS roadmap for companies and NBFCs, including net worth.
Identify statutory provisions and the Division II format of Schedule III.

meta.exam_tip: For roadmap questions, compute net worth first, then apply listing status and group relationships.

concepts.title: Why India moved from AS to Ind AS
body: Accounting standards set principles for recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure so that financial statements are reliable and comparable. In India the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of ICAI drafts them; the Central Government notifies them for companies on NFRA's recommendation, and ICAI issues them for non-corporate entities.

Before Ind AS, Indian companies followed the AS framework (27 standards in force). AS struggled with newer complexities: compound and convertible instruments, embedded and commodity derivatives, group restructurings, digital-age revenue models, share-based pay, complex deferred tax and limited disclosures on revenue, related parties and segments.

With growing foreign capital and cross-border listings, a framework close to global practice was needed — leading to Ind AS, converged with IFRS. Companies not covered by Ind AS (and non-corporate entities) continue with AS.
concepts.analogy: Ind AS arrived because Indian businesses became more global and complex than the old rules could describe.
concepts.work: A start-up issuing compulsorily convertible preference shares to foreign investors needs guidance AS never really gave.

concepts.title: Global standards: IASB, IFRS, convergence and adoption
body: The International Accounting Standards Committee (1973) sought to harmonise practice; in 2001 it was replaced by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) under the IFRS Foundation, which issues IFRS. An interpretations committee resolves application issues.

IOSCO's endorsement and the European Union's requirement of IFRS for listed companies from 2005 made IFRS a leading global framework alongside US GAAP; the G20 backed a single set of high-quality global standards.

Adoption means using IFRS exactly as issued; convergence means aligning national standards with IFRS while allowing changes for local conditions. India chose convergence: Ind AS are largely IFRS with some "carve-outs" (departures) and "carve-ins" (additions).
Benefits: comparability across countries, lower cost of capital for cross-border fund-raising, easier group reporting, better disclosure and investor confidence.
concepts.analogy: India speaks the global accounting language with a local accent — convergence, not word-for-word adoption.
concepts.work: Ind AS allows certain choices (carve-outs) that IFRS does not, to suit Indian law and practice.

concepts.title: How Ind AS are made, numbered and structured
body: Process: the ASB studies the IFRS, identifies needed changes, issues an exposure draft for public comment, finalises the standard, and the ICAI Council approves and recommends it to NFRA; NFRA reviews and recommends it to the Central Government (MCA), which notifies it in the Official Gazette under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015.

Numbering follows IFRS: standards derived from IAS keep IAS numbers (Ind AS 1 to 41), and those from IFRS are numbered from 101 (e.g. Ind AS 101 first-time adoption, Ind AS 115 revenue, Ind AS 116 leases, Ind AS 117 insurance contracts). Interpretations appear as appendices to the related Ind AS.

Typical structure: objective, scope, definitions, recognition, measurement, presentation, disclosure, effective date and transition, with appendices (application guidance and integral material) — and a comparison with IFRS explaining carve-outs.
concepts.analogy: Knowing the numbering lets you jump straight from an IFRS reference to the matching Ind AS.
concepts.work: IFRS 15 becomes Ind AS 115; IAS 16 becomes Ind AS 16.

concepts.title: Roadmap for applying Ind AS
body: Companies — Phase I (periods from 1 April 2016): listed or about-to-be-listed companies, and unlisted companies, with net worth of ₹500 crore or more. Phase II (from 1 April 2017): all other listed companies, and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250–500 crore. Holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies of covered companies follow them. Companies listed on SME exchanges are outside the roadmap. Voluntary early adoption is allowed for other companies.

Net worth (section 2(57)): paid-up capital plus reserves created out of profits and securities premium, minus accumulated losses and any deferred or miscellaneous expenditure still carried on the balance sheet; reserves from revaluation, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation are excluded. It is measured on standalone figures as at 31 March 2014 (or the first audited statements after that for newer companies).

NBFCs: Phase I from 1 April 2018 (net worth ₹500 crore or more); Phase II from 1 April 2019 (listed NBFCs below ₹500 crore and unlisted NBFCs of ₹250–500 crore); others stay on AS and cannot adopt voluntarily. Scheduled commercial banks and insurers follow separate timelines set by their regulators.

Key transition rules: one year's comparatives under Ind AS, so the transition date is the start of the comparative year; standards effective at the end of the first Ind AS period apply; once applied, Ind AS cannot be abandoned; it applies to both standalone and consolidated statements; overseas group entities may prepare standalone statements under local law if the Indian parent consolidates under Ind AS.
concepts.analogy: Size and listing decide when Ind AS arrived — and once in, there is no way back.
concepts.work: A subsidiary of a Phase I company had to adopt Ind AS in 2016 even if it was tiny.

concepts.title: Statutory framework and Division II of Schedule III
body: Section 129 requires financial statements to give a true and fair view and comply with notified standards in the form of Schedule III; section 133 empowers the Central Government to prescribe standards recommended by ICAI after NFRA's examination. SEBI's regulations require listed entities to publish results in the format and under the standards applicable.

Schedule III Division II sets the format for Ind AS companies: a balance sheet (assets, equity and liabilities split into current and non-current), a statement showing movements in equity, a profit and loss statement that also carries other comprehensive income (items that will and will not be reclassified to profit or loss), and notes. Division I is for AS companies; Division III for Ind AS NBFCs.

ICAI's Guidance Note on Division II explains presentation issues such as classification of financial liabilities, other equity components and additional disclosures (e.g. ageing of receivables and payables, ratios, undisclosed income and crypto holdings).
concepts.analogy: Schedule III is the shape of the box; Ind AS decides what goes into it.
concepts.work: Gains on remeasuring defined benefit plans go to OCI and are shown as items that will not be reclassified.

illustrations.title: Does the roadmap catch this company?
illustrations.q: Orion Ltd. (listed) had at 31 March 2014 (₹ crore): equity capital 200; securities premium 80; general reserve 150; retained earnings 120; revaluation reserve 60; capital reserve arising on amalgamation 20; miscellaneous expenditure not written off 15. Compute net worth for the Ind AS roadmap and identify the phase.

head: Item
Treatment
₹ crore
rows: Reserves created out of profits — include
solution.title: Net worth — section 2(57)

solution.text: Listed with net worth of ₹535 crore (₹500 crore or more), Orion falls in Phase I: Ind AS from accounting periods beginning 1 April 2016, with comparatives for 2015-16 and transition date 1 April 2015. Its group companies (holding, subsidiaries, joint ventures, associates) are covered too.

illustrations.title: Dates on first adoption
illustrations.q: Pinnacle Pvt. Ltd. (unlisted, net worth ₹120 crore) decides to adopt Ind AS voluntarily for the year ending 31 March 2028. Identify its first Ind AS reporting period, comparative period, date of transition and which version of Ind AS it applies. Can it later revert to AS if net worth falls?

head: Point
Answer
rows: Date of transition (opening Ind AS balance sheet)
Ind AS effective at the end of the first Ind AS reporting period (31 March 2028)
Not allowed — once Ind AS is applied, voluntarily or mandatorily, it continues for all later periods

jobs.title: Ind AS applicability memo
jobs.situation: A private group with a listed parent asks which entities must use Ind AS.
steps: Identify the parent's phase from listing and net worth.
List all subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures.
Apply the group rule to each Indian entity.
Note overseas entities that may use local GAAP for standalone accounts.
jobs.takeaway: Ind AS travels through the group — check every related company, not just the parent.

mcqs.q: Ind AS are best described as:
options: Converged with IFRS, with some carve-outs and carve-ins
mcqs.explain: India chose convergence: Ind AS track IFRS but depart where Indian conditions require. In practice: read the comparison appendix to each Ind AS.
mcqs.topic: Global standards: IASB, IFRS, convergence and adoption

mcqs.q: Ind AS are notified for companies by:
options: The Central Government (MCA) on NFRA's recommendation
mcqs.explain: Section 133 empowers the Government to prescribe standards recommended by ICAI after NFRA's examination. In practice: notified in the Gazette.
mcqs.topic: How Ind AS are made, numbered and structured

mcqs.q: Which Ind AS is derived from an IFRS (not an IAS)?
mcqs.explain: Standards from IFRS are numbered 101 onwards; 16, 12 and 37 come from IAS. In practice: Ind AS 115 mirrors IFRS 15.
mcqs.topic: How Ind AS are made, numbered and structured

mcqs.q: An unlisted company with net worth of ₹300 crore (31 March 2014) fell under:
mcqs.explain: Unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250–500 crore were in Phase II. In practice: its group companies followed.

mcqs.q: For roadmap net worth, which item is excluded?
mcqs.explain: Reserves from revaluation, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation do not count. In practice: deduct accumulated losses too.

mcqs.q: A company adopting Ind AS for 2028-29 has a transition date of:
mcqs.explain: One year of comparatives means the opening Ind AS balance sheet is at the start of the comparative year. In practice: restate 2027-28.

mcqs.q: An unlisted NBFC with net worth of ₹100 crore wishing to adopt Ind AS voluntarily:
options: Cannot — voluntary adoption is not allowed for NBFCs
mcqs.explain: NBFCs apply Ind AS only if they meet the roadmap criteria. In practice: they continue under AS.

mcqs.q: The Schedule III format for Ind AS companies (other than NBFCs) is:
mcqs.explain: Division I is for AS companies, Division II for Ind AS companies, Division III for Ind AS NBFCs. In practice: OCI is shown under Division II.
mcqs.topic: Statutory framework and Division II of Schedule III

mcqs.q: Once a company starts applying Ind AS:
options: It must continue even if it no longer meets the criteria
It reverts if net worth falls
mcqs.explain: The rules prohibit going back once Ind AS has been applied. In practice: plan voluntary adoption carefully.

summary: AS limits → need for IFRS-converged Ind AS.
IASB issues IFRS; India converges with carve-outs/carve-ins.
ASB → ICAI Council → NFRA → MCA notification.
Ind AS 1–41 from IAS; 101+ from IFRS.
Phase I ₹500 crore (2016); Phase II listed/₹250 crore (2017); NBFCs 2018/2019.
Schedule III Division II for Ind AS companies.
remember: No reverting to AS once Ind AS applied.
Transition date = start of comparative year.
traps: Revaluation reserve excluded from net worth.

viva.q: Distinguish adoption and convergence of IFRS.
viva.model: Adoption uses IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB; convergence aligns national standards with IFRS while permitting departures for local conditions, as India did.

viva.q: Outline how an Ind AS is notified.
viva.model: ASB drafts and exposes it, the ICAI Council approves and recommends it, NFRA examines and recommends it, and the Central Government notifies it.

viva.q: Which companies were in Phase I?
viva.model: Companies, listed or unlisted, whose net worth was 500 crore rupees or more, together with their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies, from 1 April 2016.

viva.q: How is net worth computed for the roadmap?
viva.model: Paid-up capital plus reserves from profits and securities premium, less accumulated losses and unwritten-off expenditure, excluding revaluation, depreciation write-back and amalgamation reserves.

viva.q: What does Division II of Schedule III contain?
viva.model: Formats for an Ind AS company's balance sheet, its statement of changes in equity, and its profit and loss statement with other comprehensive income, plus the related notes.

cases.title: The Vega group
cases.case: Vega Holdings Ltd. (listed, net worth ₹650 crore at 31 March 2014) has: Vega Retail Pvt. Ltd. (Indian subsidiary, net worth ₹40 crore); Vega Finance Ltd. (unlisted NBFC subsidiary, net worth ₹180 crore); and Vega Europe GmbH (German subsidiary).

mcqs.q: Vega Holdings applied Ind AS from:
mcqs.explain: Listed with net worth above ₹500 crore — Phase I. In practice: transition date 1 April 2015.

options: Must apply Ind AS as a subsidiary of a Phase I company
Continues with AS due to its small size
mcqs.explain: Subsidiaries of covered companies follow the parent's phase regardless of size. In practice: both standalone and consolidated.

options: May follow German requirements, provided the parent consolidates under Ind AS
mcqs.explain: Overseas group entities may prepare standalone statements under local law. In practice: Ind AS adjustments are made for consolidation.

mcqs.q: Vega Finance Ltd. is governed for Ind AS by:
options: The NBFC roadmap, as an NBFC subsidiary of a Phase I company
mcqs.explain: NBFCs follow the NBFC roadmap, which covers holding, subsidiary, JV and associate NBFCs of companies already covered. In practice: it would apply Ind AS from 1 April 2018.
